steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA) are both nucleic acids built from long chains of nucleotides, but they differ in four key ways:

1. Chemical structure  
   • Sugar: DNA’s sugar is deoxyribose (lacking one oxygen atom at the 2′ carbon), whereas RNA’s sugar is ribose (has a hydroxyl group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • Bases: Both contain adenine (A), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). DNA contains thymine (T); RNA uses uracil (U) instead.  
   • Stability: The extra –OH on ribose makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA, which lacks that group.

2. Strand architecture  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a long, antiparallel double helix stabilized by complementary base pairing (A–T, G–C).  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold into complex secondary structures (hairpins, loops) by intramolecular base pairing (A–U, G–C).

3. Functional roles  
   • DNA serves primarily as the long-term, heritable storage of genetic information in cells.  
   • RNA has diverse roles: messenger RNA (mRNA) carries genetic information to ribosomes; ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA) are integral to protein synthesis; and many other RNAs (e.g., microRNA, siRNA, snRNA, lncRNA) regulate gene expression, catalyze reactions (ribozymes), or act as scaffolds.

4. Cellular location and lifecycle  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA is mainly confined to the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts), replicated once per cell cycle.  
   • RNA is transcribed in the nucleus (or organelles) and often functions in the cytoplasm; it is continuously synthesized and degraded, giving it a shorter lifespan.

Together, these differences allow DNA to act as a stable genetic blueprint while RNA functions as a dynamic, versatile intermediary and regulator in the flow of genetic information.
